oneSentence: Stored information an AI system can retrieve across separate sessions to personalise, continue tasks, or reuse past facts and preferences.
plainExplanation:
In many AI systems, long-term memory means keeping selected information outside the model so it can be used again later, even after one chat or task has ended. That stored information might include a user preference, a project fact, a summary of past work, or a record of what happened in earlier steps.

What goes in is usually not the whole conversation. A separate part of the system chooses what to save, such as “send reports in French” or “the package should contain 240 boxes”. The information is then written to a memory store, which could be a database, a file, or another storage service.

What happens next is retrieval. When a new request arrives, the system searches that store for items that seem relevant and brings them back into the current working context. The model then uses that retrieved material along with the new prompt. This is different from the model’s training, which happened earlier and affects its general behaviour rather than one user’s stored information.

What comes out is a response or action that can reflect earlier interactions across time. This can make systems more useful, but it also creates risks. A saved detail may be wrong, outdated, biased, or too sensitive to store. That is why long-term memory needs clear rules about what may be saved, how long it stays, who can inspect it, and when a human should review or correct it.

everydayAnalogy.title: The regular order card
everydayAnalogy.story: A café does not need to record every conversation with a regular customer. It may keep one useful note on an order card, such as “usually asks for tea without sugar”. On the next visit, staff retrieve that note when the customer gives their name. The note saves time, but it is not automatically true forever. If the customer changes their order, someone must update or remove it. An AI memory works similarly: it captures information, selects what may be useful later, stores it and retrieves it when a relevant new request arrives.

mapping.analogyElement: few lasting notes instead of every conversation
mapping.aiElement: selective saving of useful information rather than storing all context

mapping.analogyElement: next shift retrieves relevant notes for today’s container
mapping.aiElement: new session retrieves relevant memory for the current task

mapping.analogyElement: old note causing a repeated mistake
mapping.aiElement: stale or incorrect memory influencing later outputs

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A warehouse logbook is usually written and read by people who understand the notes directly. In AI systems, memory often has to be transformed into a searchable format, and retrieval may be based on pattern matching rather than exact human judgement. Also, a human team can notice context that was never written down, while an AI system can only use what is retrieved into its current context.

visual.title: How long-term memory is saved and reused across sessions
visual.learningObjective: Show that long-term memory is separate from one conversation: information is selected, stored, retrieved later, and then checked before use.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with five boxes connected by arrows. It starts with a user interaction, then shows memory selection, storage, retrieval during a later session, and final response with review. Read it as a process across time, not as one continuous chat.

steps.label: 1. New interaction
steps.explanation: A user asks for help or the system observes a task. Most of this material stays only in the current session unless something is chosen for saving.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box labelled 'Current session' with example text snippets inside. Add a small clock icon to suggest temporary use.

steps.label: 2. Select what to save
steps.explanation: A rule or component decides whether a detail is worth keeping, such as a stable preference, a project fact, or a task summary.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a decision/filter box labelled 'Save?' with three tagged examples passing through and crossed-out sensitive or trivial items blocked.

steps.label: 3. Store in memory
steps.explanation: Chosen items are written to a separate memory store such as a database or file system, with labels or metadata to help later search.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a cylinder or card stack labelled 'Memory store' containing short saved items and date tags.

steps.label: 4. Retrieve later
steps.explanation: In a new session, the system searches the memory store for items relevant to the new request and brings back only some of them.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second 'Current session' box on the right. Show arrows from the memory store to this box, with only two highlighted notes moving across.

steps.label: 5. Use with checks
steps.explanation: The model uses retrieved memory with the new input, but the result may still need validation because saved information can be wrong, old, or inappropriate.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw an output box labelled 'Draft or action' followed by a warning/check badge labelled 'Verify before use'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal one example of information that should be saved and one that should not; on keyboard focus, the same text appears below the diagram.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram explains long-term memory as a five-step flow across time. First, a user interaction happens in a temporary session. Second, a filter decides whether any detail should be saved. Third, selected items are stored in a separate memory store, not inside the live chat itself. Fourth, during a later session, the system searches that store and retrieves only the items that seem relevant to the new request. Fifth, those retrieved items are used to help produce a draft or action, but a final check is needed because stored memory may be outdated, incorrect, or unsuitable to use.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-box flow appears left to right with arrows: current session, save filter, memory store, later retrieval, draft or action with verification. Retrieved items are shown as highlighted notes rather than animated movement.

workedExample.scenario: A political affairs officer uses dummy material to test whether a drafting assistant can remember non-sensitive preferences across two sessions during a procurement evaluation.
workedExample.input: First session: “For statements for delivery, use short headings and apply the programme title exactly as it appears in the supplied terminology list.” Later session: “Prepare the next section using my saved drafting preferences.”
process: The system captures the first conversation turn and the resulting draft settings.
A selection rule identifies the heading style and terminology instruction as potentially reusable. It does not save the full dummy statement.
The selected items are written to persistent storage with their source, scope and owner.
In the later session, the request for saved drafting preferences triggers retrieval of the relevant items.
The model receives the retrieved items with the new prompt and applies them to the draft. The officer can inspect, correct or delete the memory.
workedExample.result: The new section uses short headings and the supplied programme title. The system also shows which saved preferences it applied, allowing the officer to catch an obsolete term before the draft goes back into the clearance chain.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: With a statement for delivery held in the translation queue, a political affairs officer joins a procurement unit’s controlled evaluation of a drafting assistant. Using dummy text, the officer checks whether the tool can carry forward agreed terminology and formatting preferences between sessions before close of business.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The test distinguishes long-term memory from ordinary chat context. The assistant selects a durable preference, stores it outside the model and retrieves it in a later session when the officer returns to the same type of artefact.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Real draft statements, negotiating positions, vendor submissions, pricing and evaluation material must not be entered into a tool that has not been approved for them. Any enabled memory must have access controls, retention limits and a way to inspect, correct and delete stored items, otherwise an outdated or wrongly attributed preference may keep resurfacing.

whyItMatters: A system with long-term memory can feel more useful because it does not start from zero every time. It can continue work across days, reuse stable preferences, and reduce repetitive prompting. But this same feature changes the risk profile. Once information is stored and reused, mistakes can persist, sensitive details can spread too far, and old assumptions can shape new outputs without being noticed. For policy, procurement, and human-rights work, the key questions are governance questions: what may be stored, for how long, with whose knowledge, under what access controls, and with what route for correction, deletion, and human review. If you ignore long-term memory, you may misunderstand what the system is actually using to produce an answer or action.

An ICT governance board review of retention settings
A front-office discussion before enabling a drafting assistant
A data protection review of an agent’s memory store

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Long-term memory means the model permanently learned something new.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually it means the system saved information in an external store and retrieved it later. That can change a future response without changing the model’s underlying trained parameters. Training changes the model itself; memory changes what information is supplied to it at runtime.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a system has memory, it remembers everything automatically.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Most systems cannot keep everything, and storing everything would often be risky or inefficient. Designers usually choose what to save, how long to keep it, and what to retrieve. Many details from a conversation may never enter long-term memory at all.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Stored memory is more reliable than the current conversation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A saved item can be incomplete, outdated, wrongly extracted, or taken out of context. Retrieval can also bring back the wrong item. Memory can improve continuity, but it does not guarantee correctness.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is like a saved notebook for an AI system. Some useful details from earlier interactions are written down somewhere outside the chat, so they can be brought back in a later session.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In many AI systems, long-term memory uses persistent storage outside the model, such as databases, document stores, key-value stores, or vector databases. A memory pipeline usually has four parts: capture, selection, storage, and retrieval. During capture, the system receives conversation turns, tool results, or task outcomes. During selection, the system uses rules, classifiers, or prompts to identify what is worth persisting, such as user preferences, entity facts, summaries, plans, or prior actions. During storage, those items are saved with metadata such as source, timestamp, permissions, and scope. During retrieval, the system uses keys, filters, search, similarity matching, or hybrid methods to fetch records relevant to a new request. The retrieved items are then inserted into the current context window or passed through tools for downstream use. This differs from short-term memory, which only holds information for the current interaction, and from training, which updates model parameters rather than storing per-user or per-task records.

keyTakeaway: Long-term memory is persistent information retrieved across sessions, not a change to the model itself. It improves continuity, but stored items need controls for access, retention, correction and deletion.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes long-term memory in many AI systems?
options: It is extra space inside one chat so the model can read more tokens at once.
It is stored information outside the model that can be retrieved in later sessions.
It is the model permanently updating itself after every user message.
It is a guarantee that the system will remember facts accurately forever.
quickCheck.explanation: In many systems, long-term memory means persistent storage outside the model, later retrieved when relevant. It is not the same as a larger context window, automatic retraining after each message, or guaranteed accuracy.

issues.problem: The opening defines long-term memory universally as information kept outside the model. That describes a common agent architecture, but not every AI system with persistent memory. The later technical section correctly limits the claim to “many AI systems”.
issues.fix: Replace the opening with: “In many AI systems, long-term memory means keeping selected information outside the model so it can be used again later, even after one chat or task has ended.”

issues.problem: The statement that “prompts decide what is worth persisting” is false and assigns agency to a prompt. A prompt can guide model processing, but it does not itself make a selection.
issues.fix: Replace that sentence with: “During selection, the system uses rules, classifiers, or prompts to identify what is worth persisting, such as user preferences, entity facts, summaries, plans, or prior actions.”
